{{short description|Abstract algebra concept}}
In [[abstract algebra]], a '''decomposition of a module''' is a way to write a [[module (mathematics)|module]] as a [[direct sum of modules]]. A type of a decomposition is often used to define or [[characterization (mathematics)|characterize]] modules: for example, a [[semisimple module]] is a module that has a decomposition into [[simple module]]s. Given a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]], the types of decomposition of modules over the ring can also be used to define or characterize the ring: a ring is semisimple [[if and only if]] every module over it is a semisimple module.

An [[indecomposable module]] is a module that is not a direct sum of two nonzero [[submodule]]s. '''Azumaya's theorem''' states that if a module has an decomposition into modules with [[local ring|local]] [[endomorphism ring]]s, then all decompositions into indecomposable modules are equivalent to each other; a special case of this, especially in [[group theory]], is known as the [[Krull–Schmidt theorem]].

A special case of a decomposition of a module is a decomposition of a ring: for example, a ring is semisimple if and only if it is a direct sum (in fact a [[product ring|product]]) of [[matrix ring]]s over [[division ring]]s (this observation is known as the [[Artin–Wedderburn theorem]]).

== Idempotents and decompositions ==
{{main|Idempotent element}}

To give a direct sum decomposition of a module into submodules is the same as to give [[Idempotent (ring theory)#Types of ring idempotents|orthogonal idempotents]] in the [[endomorphism ring]] of the module that sum up to the [[identity map]].<ref>{{harvnb|Anderson|Fuller|1992|loc=Corollary 6.19. and Corollary 6.20.}}</ref> Indeed, if <math display="inline">M = \bigoplus_{i \in I} M_i</math>, then, for each <math>i \in I</math>, the [[module homomorphism|linear]] [[endomorphism]] <math>e_i : M \to M_i \hookrightarrow M</math> given by the natural projection followed by the natural inclusion is an [[idempotent (ring theory)|idempotent]]. They are clearly orthogonal to each other (<math>e_i e_j = 0</math> for <math>i \ne j</math>) and they sum up to the identity map:
:<math>1_{\operatorname{M}} = \sum_{i \in I} e_i</math>
as endomorphisms (here the summation is well-defined since it is a finite sum at each element of the module). [[Converse (logic)|Conversely]], each set of orthogonal idempotents <math>\{ e_i \}_{i \in I}</math> such that only finitely many <math>e_i(x)</math> are nonzero for each <math>x \in M</math> and <math display="inline”>\sum e_i = 1_M</math> determine a direct sum decomposition by taking <math>M_i</math> to be the [[image (mathematics)|images]] of <math>e_i</math>.

This fact already puts some constraints on a possible decomposition of a ring: given a ring <math>R</math>, suppose there is a decomposition
:<math>{}_R R = \bigoplus_{a \in A} I_a</math>
of <math>R</math> as a left module over itself, where <math>I_a</math> are left submodules; i.e., left [[ideal (ring theory)|ideals]]. Each endomorphism <math>{}_R R \to {}_R R</math> can be identified with a right multiplication by an element of ''R''; thus, <math>I_a = R e_a</math> where <math>e_a</math> are idempotents of <math>\operatorname{End}({}_R R) \simeq R</math>.<ref>Here, the endomorphism ring is thought of as acting from the right; if it acts from the left, this identification is for the opposite ring of ''R''.</ref> The summation of idempotent endomorphisms corresponds to the decomposition of the unity of ''R'': <math display="inline">1_R = \sum_{a \in A} e_a \in \bigoplus_{a \in A} I_a</math>, which is necessarily a finite sum; in particular, <math>A</math> must be a finite set.

For example, take <math>R = \operatorname{M}_n(D)</math>, the ring of ''n''-by-''n'' [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] over a division ring ''D''. Then <math>{}_R R</math> is the direct sum of ''n'' copies of <math>D^n</math>, the columns; each column is a simple left ''R''-submodule or, in other words, a [[minimal ideal|minimal left ideal]].<ref>{{harvnb|Procesi|2007|loc=Ch.6., § 1.3.}}</ref>

Let ''R'' be a ring. Suppose there is a (necessarily finite) decomposition of it as a left module over itself
:<math>{}_R R = R_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus R_n</math>
into ''two-sided ideals'' <math>R_i</math> of ''R''. As above, <math>R_i = R e_i</math> for some orthogonal idempotents <math>e_i</math> such that <math>\textstyle{1 = \sum_1^n e_i}</math>. Since <math>R_i</math> is an ideal, <math>e_i R \subset R_i</math> and so <math>e_i R e_j \subset R_i \cap R_j = 0</math> for <math>i \ne j</math>. Then, for each ''i'',
:<math>e_i r = \sum_j e_j r e_i = \sum_j e_i r e_j = r e_i.</math>
That is, the <math>e_i</math> are in the [[center (ring theory)|center]]; i.e., they are [[central idempotent]]s.<ref>{{harvnb|Anderson|Fuller|1992|loc=Proposion 7.6.}}</ref> Clearly, the argument can be reversed and so there is a one-to-one correspondence between the direct sum decomposition into ideals and the orthogonal central idempotents summing up to the unity 1. Also, each <math>R_i</math> itself is a ring on its own right, the unity given by <math>e_i</math>, and, as a ring, ''R'' is the product ring <math>R_1 \times \cdots \times R_n.</math>

For example, again take <math>R = \operatorname{M}_n(D)</math>. This ring is a simple ring; in particular, it has no nontrivial decomposition into two-sided ideals.

== Types of decomposition ==
There are several types of direct sum decompositions that have been studied:
*[[Semisimple decomposition]]: a direct sum of simple modules.
*'''Indecomposable decomposition''': a direct sum of indecomposable modules.
*A decomposition with local endomorphism rings<ref>{{harv|Jacobson|2009|loc=A paragraph before Theorem 3.6.}} calls a module ''strongly indecomposable'' if nonzero and has local endomorphism ring.</ref> (cf. [[#Azumaya's theorem]]): a direct sum of modules whose endomorphism rings are [[local ring]]s (a ring is local if for each element ''x'', either ''x'' or 1 − ''x'' is a [[unit (ring theory)|unit]]).
*'''Serial decomposition''': a direct sum of [[uniserial module]]s (a module is uniserial if the lattice of submodules is a finite chain<ref>{{harvnb|Anderson|Fuller|1992|loc=§ 32.}}</ref>).

Since a simple module is indecomposable, a semisimple decomposition is an indecomposable decomposition (but not conversely). If the endomorphism ring of a module is local, then, in particular, it cannot have a nontrivial idempotent: the module is indecomposable. Thus, a decomposition with local endomorphism rings is an indecomposable decomposition.

A direct summand is said to be ''maximal'' if it admits an indecomposable complement. A decomposition <math>\textstyle{M = \bigoplus_{i \in I} M_i}</math> is said to ''complement maximal direct summands'' if for each maximal direct summand ''L'' of ''M'', there exists a subset <math>J \subset I</math> such that 
:<math>M = \left(\bigoplus_{j \in J} M_j \right) \bigoplus L.</math><ref name="Anderson 12">{{harvnb|Anderson|Fuller|1992|loc=§ 12.}}</ref> 
<!-- true but a wrong place: For example, a ring is a [[semiperfect ring]] if and only if every projective module over the ring has an indecomposable decomposition complementing maximal direct summands. -->

Two decompositions <math>M = \bigoplus_{i \in I} M_i = \bigoplus_{j \in J} N_j</math> are said to be ''equivalent'' if there is a [[bijection]] <math>\varphi : I \overset{\sim}\to J</math> such that for each <math>i \in I</math>, <math>M_i \simeq N_{\varphi(i)}</math>.<ref name="Anderson 12" /> If a module admits an indecomposable decomposition complementing maximal direct summands, then any two indecomposable decompositions of the module are equivalent.<ref>{{harvnb|Anderson|Fuller|1992|loc=Theorrm 12.4.}}</ref>

== Azumaya's theorem ==

In the simplest form, '''Azumaya's theorem''' states:<ref>{{harvnb|Facchini|1998|loc=Theorem 2.12.}}</ref> given a decomposition <math>M = \bigoplus_{i \in I} M_i</math> such that the endomorphism ring of each <math>M_i</math> is [[local ring|local]] (so the decomposition is indecomposable), each indecomposable decomposition of ''M'' is equivalent to this given decomposition. The more precise version of the theorem states:<ref>{{harvnb|Anderson|Fuller|1992|loc=Theorem 12.6. and Lemma 26.4.}}</ref> still given such a decomposition, if <math>M = N \oplus K</math>, then
# if nonzero, ''N'' contains an indecomposable direct summand,
# if <math>N</math> is indecomposable, the endomorphism ring of it is local<ref>{{harvnb|Facchini|1998|loc=Lemma 2.11.}}</ref> and <math>K</math> is complemented by the given decomposition:
#:<math display="inline">M = M_j \oplus K</math> and so <math>M_j \simeq N</math> for some <math>j \in I</math>,
# for each <math>i \in I</math>, there exist direct summands <math>N'</math> of <math>N</math> and <math>K'</math> of <math>K</math> such that <math>M = M_i \oplus N' \oplus K'</math>.

The endomorphism ring of an indecomposable module of finite [[length of a module|length]] is local (e.g., by [[Fitting's lemma]]) and thus Azumaya's theorem applies to the setup of the [[Krull–Schmidt theorem]]. Indeed, if ''M'' is a module of finite length, then, by [[mathematical induction|induction]] on length, it has a finite indecomposable decomposition <math display="inline">M = \bigoplus_{i=1}^n M_i</math>, which is a decomposition with local endomorphism rings. Now, suppose we are given an indecomposable decomposition <math display="inline">M = \bigoplus_{i=1}^m N_i</math>. Then it must be equivalent to the first one: so <math>m = n</math> and <math>M_i \simeq N_{\sigma(i)}</math> for some [[permutation]] <math>\sigma</math> of <math>\{ 1, \dots, n \}</math>. More precisely, since <math>N_1</math> is indecomposable, <math display="inline">M = M_{i_1} \bigoplus (\bigoplus_{i=2}^n N_i)</math> for some <math>i_1</math>. Then, since <math>N_2</math> is indecomposable, <math display="inline">M = M_{i_1} \bigoplus M_{i_2} \bigoplus (\bigoplus_{i=3}^n N_i)</math> and so on; i.e., complements to each sum <math display="inline">\bigoplus_{i=l}^n N_i</math> can be taken to be direct sums of some <math>M_i</math>'s.

Another application is the following statement (which is a key step in the [[mathematical proof|proof]] of [[Kaplansky's theorem on projective modules]]):
*Given an element <math>x \in N</math>, there exist a direct summand <math>H</math> of <math>N</math> and a subset <math>J \subset I</math> such that <math>x \in H</math> and <math display="inline">H \simeq \bigoplus_{j \in J} M_j</math>.
To see this, choose a finite set <math>F \subset I</math> such that <math display="inline">x \in \bigoplus_{j \in F} M_j</math>. Then, writing <math>M = N \oplus L</math>, by Azumaya's theorem, <math>M = (\oplus_{j \in F} M_j) \oplus N_1 \oplus L_1</math> with some direct summands <math>N_1, L_1</math> of <math>N, L</math> and then, by [[modular law]], <math>N = H \oplus N_1</math> with <math>H = (\oplus_{j \in F} M_j \oplus L_1) \cap N</math>. Then, since <math>L_1</math> is a direct summand of <math>L</math>, we can write <math>L = L_1 \oplus L_1'</math> and then <math>\oplus_{j \in F} M_j \simeq H \oplus L_1'</math>, which implies, since ''F'' is finite, that <math>H \simeq \oplus_{j \in J} M_j</math> for some ''J'' by a repeated application of Azumaya's theorem.

In the setup of Azumaya's theorem, if, in addition, each <math>M_i</math> is [[countably generated module|countably generated]], then there is the following refinement (due originally to Crawley–Jónsson and later to Warfield): <math>N</math> is [[isomorphic]] to <math>\bigoplus_{j \in J} M_j</math> for some subset <math>J \subset I</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Facchini|1998|loc=Corollary 2.55.}}</ref> (In a sense, this is an extension of Kaplansky's theorem and is proved by the two lemmas used in the proof of the theorem.) According to {{harv|Facchini|1998}}, it is not known whether the assumption "<math>M_i</math> countably generated" can be dropped; i.e., this refined version is true in general.

== Decomposition of a ring ==
On the decomposition of a ring, the most basic but still important observation, known as the [[Wedderburn-Artin theorem]] is this: given a ring ''R'', the following are equivalent:
# ''R'' is a [[semisimple ring]]; i.e., <math>{}_R R</math> is a semisimple left module.
# <math>R \cong \prod_{i=1}^r \operatorname{M}_{m_i}(D_i)</math> for [[division ring]]s <math>D_1, \dots, D_r</math>, where <math>\operatorname{M}_n(D_i)</math> denotes the ring of ''n''-by-''n'' matrices with entries in <math>D_i</math>, and the positive [[integer]]s <math>r</math>, the division rings <math>D_1, \dots , D_r</math>, and the positive integers <math>m_1, \dots, m_r</math> are determined (the latter two up to permutation) by ''R'' 
# Every left module over ''R'' is semisimple.

To show 1. <math>\Rightarrow</math> 2., first note that if <math>R</math> is semisimple then we have an isomorphism of left <math>R</math>-modules <math display="inline">{}_R R \cong \bigoplus_{i=1}^r I_i^{\oplus m_i}</math> where <math>I_i</math> are mutually non-isomorphic minimal left ideals.  Then, with the view that endomorphisms act from the right,
:<math>R \cong \operatorname{End}({}_R R) \cong \bigoplus_{i=1}^r \operatorname{End}(I_i^{\oplus m_i})</math>
where each <math>\operatorname{End}(I_i^{\oplus m_i})</math> can be viewed as the matrix ring over  <math>D_i = \operatorname{End}(I_i)</math>, which is a division ring by [[Schur's Lemma]].  The converse holds because the decomposition of 2. is equivalent to a decomposition into minimal left ideals = simple left submodules. The equivalence 1. <math>\Leftrightarrow</math> 3. holds because every module is a [[quotient module|quotient]] of a [[free module]], and a quotient of a semisimple module is semisimple.
